title: Un export de 44 secondes : mesurer avant de chercher
title_hi: Un export de 44 secondes : mesurer avant de chercher
summary: Quand je tombe sur une lenteur, j'écris d'abord trois choses : ce que j'instrumente, ce que je compare, et ce qui me fer
content:
Quand je tombe sur une lenteur, j'écris d'abord trois choses : ce que j'instrumente, ce que je compare, et ce qui me ferait abandonner mon hypothèse. Dix minutes. Sans ça, je pars sur la première piste qui a l'air logique, et ça ne veut pas dire que c'est la bonne.

Trois exemples.


  
  
  L'export de 44 secondes


Un export mettait 44 secondes. J'ai mesuré avant de supposer : plus de 42 secondes se passaient côté application, avant même l'appel au service. Le service, lui, répondait en un peu plus d'une seconde.

Le coupable : des requêtes en cascade. Un exemple générique, ce n'est pas le code d'origine :



# 1 requête pour les comptes, puis 1 par compte
accounts.each { |a| puts a.employees.count }

# 2 requêtes, quel que soit le nombre de comptes
accounts.includes(:employees).each { |a| puts a.employees.size }







  
  
  Les plus gros comptes


Une autre lenteur, uniquement sur les très gros comptes. Je suis reparti de zéro : j'ai instrumenté le front et le back, puis comparé trois tailles de compte. Ce qui grossit avec le compte, c'est le goulot.

J'ai corrigé les requêtes en cascade plutôt que d'ajouter du cache, parce qu'un cache masque le problème sans le régler. Le correctif backend est en production, et j'ai recensé les autres endroits qui avaient le même défaut.


  
  
  Le bug d'affichage


Ça ressemblait à un bug d'interface. En remontant, c'était un contournement d'une règle métier. Ce qui a tranché : aucune vue de l'application ne permet de créer cet état à la main, donc il venait d'ailleurs. Le sujet n'était plus l'affichage, c'était une décision à prendre un niveau au-dessus.

Et si une analyse que j'ai postée se révèle fausse, je la corrige au même endroit.

Le reste de ma façon de travailler est sur amineaffif.com/methode.

Amine Affif, développeur full-stack à Paris.

English version: A 44-second export: measure before you look

title: A 44-second export: measure before you look
title_hi: A 44-second export: measure before you look
summary: When I hit a slowdown, I write three things down first: what I instrument, what I compare, and what would make me drop m
content:
When I hit a slowdown, I write three things down first: what I instrument, what I compare, and what would make me drop my hypothesis. Ten minutes. Without it, I follow the first lead that looks logical, and that doesn't make it the right one.

Three examples.


  
  
  The 44-second export


An export took 44 seconds. I measured before assuming: more than 42 seconds were spent in the application, before the call to the service even started. The service itself answered in a little over a second.

The culprit: cascading queries. A generic example, not the original code:



# 1 query for the accounts, then 1 per account
accounts.each { |a| puts a.employees.count }

# 2 queries, whatever the number of accounts
accounts.includes(:employees).each { |a| puts a.employees.size }







  
  
  The biggest accounts


Another slowdown, only on the very large accounts. I started over: I instrumented the front end and the back end, then compared three account sizes. What grows with the account is the bottleneck.

I fixed the cascading queries instead of adding a cache, because a cache hides the problem without solving it. The backend fix is in production, and I went through the other places with the same flaw.


  
  
  The display bug


It looked like a UI bug. Digging back, it was a business rule being bypassed. What settled it: no screen in the app lets you create that state by hand, so it came from somewhere else. The subject was no longer the display, it was a decision for someone a level up.

And if an analysis I posted turns out to be wrong, I correct it in the same place.

The rest of how I work is at amineaffif.com/en/methode.

Amine Affif, full-stack developer in Paris.

Version française : Un export de 44 secondes : mesurer avant de chercher

title: My keyword search took 5 seconds over 355k jobs, and C++ matched random jobs
title_hi: My keyword search took 5 seconds over 355k jobs, and C++ matched random jobs
summary: I'm building a searchable index of about 310,000 open jobs from roughly 6,800 company career pages, mostly Indian IT a
content:
I'm building a searchable index of about 310,000 open jobs from roughly 6,800 company career pages, mostly Indian IT and services firms. Most of them publish their openings through public job feeds, so I pull from those.


  
  
  The 5-second search


My first keyword search used ILIKE over title and company. On 355k rows, EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed a full sequential scan at about 5 seconds, which is too slow for a search box.

Trigram indexes fixed the speed but used too much storage on the free tier. I switched to a GIN index over to_tsvector('simple', ...). I chose simple over english because english stems words and drops stopwords, which makes results hard to predict.


  
  
  The C++ problem


With the new index, searching for C++ returned unrelated jobs. Postgres reduces C++ to a bare c token under both text configs, and .NET to net. So a C++ search matched anything with a standalone "c" in it.

The fix is a normalization step applied on both sides of the search:



c++ → cpp


c# → csharp


.net → dotnet



It runs in the index expression and in the query builder, so they stay in sync. The catch is that these rules live in two places, and I have to keep them matching by hand.


  
  
  Rate limiting, what didn't work


My first limiter was a globalThis Map on Vercel. Every cold start reset it, so it wasn't really a limit. Cloudflare's native rate-limit binding didn't enforce for me either. I sent 220+ requests and got zero 429s.

A Durable Object keyed by API key (idFromName(apiKey)) worked. It started returning 429 around request 62, and other keys weren't affected.


  
  
  Hyperdrive setup gotchas



Use Supabase's direct connection (port 5432). Hyperdrive does its own pooling.
Use one pg Client per request.
On Supabase, GRANT postgres TO hyperdrive_user isn't allowed. I granted scoped SELECT and added an RLS policy for that role only.



  
  
  What it doesn't do



No job descriptions. Title, company, location, apply link, and dates only.
Refreshes about once a day. Each row has lastSeenAt.
About a third of rows have no city.
No salary. The sources don't publish it consistently.


If you've run a similar setup, I'd like to know how you handled keyword search over a large table without a trigram index.

The Actor is here if you want to look at the data: https://apify.com/pk07007/ats-jobs-api

title: A practical checklist for self-hosting website forms
title_hi: A practical checklist for self-hosting website forms
summary: A contact form is often treated as a small front-end feature. In practice it is a data pipeline: the browser sends a req
content:
A contact form is often treated as a small front-end feature. In practice it is a data pipeline: the browser sends a request, an API validates it, storage retains it, and a human or workflow acts on it. If any step fails silently, a lead or support request disappears.

I build software at NodeDR, including a self-hosted form backend. Here is the checklist I would use before moving forms onto infrastructure I control.


  
  
  1. Draw the path of one submission


Write down the path from the visitor's browser to the person who reads the result. Include DNS, TLS, reverse proxy, application, database, notification channel, and any file store. This makes outages and ownership boundaries visible.

Also decide what happens when a notification fails. A Telegram or email alert is convenient, but it should not be the only copy of the submission. The durable record should be queryable in the dashboard or database.


  
  
  2. Separate public and secret keys


The browser needs permission to submit to a form. It should never need an administrative credential. Use a project-scoped public key for browser submissions and keep secret keys on the server. If you add request signing, the signing secret belongs in a server route, not bundled JavaScript.

For multiple websites, give each project its own key. That lets you rotate one site without interrupting the others and makes abuse easier to trace.


  
  
  3. Plan for abuse before sharing the endpoint


Public forms attract automated traffic. Set request size limits, validate expected fields, and consider rate limits or a challenge for forms that get targeted. A honeypot field can help with unsophisticated bots, but it should not be the only defense. Avoid logging full submission bodies into general application logs, where personal information may be copied into more places than intended.

If visitors can upload files, decide which types and sizes are allowed, where those files live, and who can retrieve them. Prefer direct, time-limited uploads to a storage bucket over routing large file bytes through the form API.


  
  
  4. Make the failure visible to the visitor


The submit button should not always show “Success.” Treat an API error or timeout as a failure, keep the visitor's entered text in place, and offer a retry. If the API accepted the request but a later notification failed, the visitor should still see success because the submission is safely stored.

For higher-value forms, include a submission identifier in the response. It helps support teams investigate a missing notification without searching through personal data.


  
  
  5. Test exports and restore, not just backups


Owning the database is useful only if you can retrieve and restore its contents. Test a small export before launch. Decide whether you need CSV/XLSX for operations, a database dump for disaster recovery, or both. Store backups separately from the live host and practice restoring into a clean environment.

Write down retention rules, too. A form backend may collect names, email addresses, and free-text messages. Decide when old submissions should be deleted and who can access them.


  
  
  6. Check the operational cost


Self-hosting replaces a subscription with your own operational work: updates, monitoring, backups, security patches, and incident response. That trade can be worthwhile for data control or predictable volume, but it should be explicit. Start with one low-risk form, observe how it behaves, and only then move the forms that matter most.


  
  
  A concrete option


We built Submify around this model. It provides a self-hosted API and dashboard, per-project keys, PostgreSQL storage, exports, optional S3-compatible file uploads, and notifications. It is AGPL-3.0 licensed, with its source on GitHub. I am affiliated with the project, so treat it as one implementation to evaluate against the checklist rather than a universal answer.

What failure mode has caused you the most trouble with website forms: delivery, spam, exports, or something else?

content:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend


  
  
  What I Built


A close friend of mine handles HR at a small company. Every new hire means opening the same Word salary template and copying details from emails by hand: name, designation, joining date, CTC, notice period. It's slow, and one wrong digit in a salary letter is a real problem.

So I built AI Word Template Filler: a Word add-in where she pastes an email or a few lines of text, and it fills the template for her. Nothing is written silently. Every field shows up for review first, and anything missing is flagged instead of guessed.


  
  
  Demo


  
  

[Short video: paste text → review panel → Apply to Word]


  
  
  Code


[https://github.com/krishashah-03/superdocs-builds/tree/main/extensions/krishashah-03/word-fill-template]


  
  
  How I Built It




[Open-weight model, e.g. Llama 3.3 70B] via OpenRouter extracts fields from free text like emails and bullet points

FastAPI backend normalizes dates, salary ("8 LPA" → 800000), and yes/no values, then detects gaps

React + Office.js task pane shows a review screen; only approved fields are written into Word
JSON/CSV input skips the AI entirely, so structured data stays deterministic
63 pytest tests cover parsing, normalization, gap detection, and AI error handling



  
  
  Why Open Models Matter Here




No lock-in: OpenRouter's OpenAI-compatible API let me test several open-weight models and pick the one best at structured extraction by changing one config line.

A path to fully local: because the model is open-weight, the same setup can run on her own machine through Ollama later, so salary data never has to leave the office.

Low cost: a small company can't justify an expensive API bill for filling forms; open models keep it nearly free.



  
  
  What She Said


[I've sent her a demo, and she'll try it on the next new joiner's salary letter. I'll update this section with her honest verdict, good or bad]


  
  
  What's Next


Offer letters and NDAs. The engine is schema-driven, so a new template only needs a new schema.json.

title: "Can I ignore this?" — I built Handle It NL for a friend navigating Dutch letters
title_hi: "Can I ignore this?" — I built Handle It NL for a friend navigating Dutch letters
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend.


  
  
  What I Built


I built Handl
content:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend.


  
  
  What I Built


I built Handle It NL, a Dutch-letter problem solver for expats in the Netherlands.

I built it for my wife, she recently moved to Netherlands and she is learning dutch but sometimes she finds it difficult with the letters from municipality or government.

The interesting part was that translation was not really the whole problem.

Someone can translate a Dutch letter perfectly into English and still be left asking:


“Okay... but what am I actually supposed to do?”


Is it serious?

Can I ignore it?

Do I need to pay something?

Is there a deadline?

Do I have to visit somewhere?

What should I bring?

What happens if I do nothing?

That became the idea behind Handle It NL.

Instead of acting as another translation tool, it tries to turn a Dutch letter into an explanation, a decision, and a safe next action.

A user uploads:


a photo;
a screenshot;
a JPG/PNG/WEBP image;
or a scanned PDF.


Handle It NL then classifies the document as:


Payment required
Appointment / visit
Action required
Information only
Mixed
Needs review


The UI focuses on four questions:



WHAT IS THIS?

CAN I IGNORE IT?

WHAT DO I NEED TO DO?

BY WHEN?






It can also extract:


sender;
subject;
payment amount;
payment reference;
deadline;
appointment date/time;
visit location;
documents or items to bring;
consequence of ignoring the letter when supported;
useful Dutch administrative terms.


But the part I found most interesting was what happens after the model understands the letter.

Handle It NL can decide that a real tool would be useful.

For example, it can:


verify a Dutch address through PDOK;
prepare an .ics calendar event;
create a Google Calendar link;
save an appointment or deadline locally;
look up curated guidance for selected Dutch administrative processes.


And sometimes the correct action is simply:



NO ACTION NEEDED






For example, an informational neighbourhood notice should not create a deadline or calendar event just because an AI agent happens to have tools available.

That ability to decide when not to act became an important part of the project.





  
  
  The rule behind the application


One rule became central while I was building Handle It NL:


The model interprets. Deterministic tools execute.


The language model is allowed to understand the document and decide which capability may help.

But it does not get to pretend that an action happened.

For example:


PDOK determines whether an address was actually verified;
Python generates the real .ics file;
SQLite determines whether a deadline was really stored;
the backend determines whether an appointment already exists;
the UI shows tool results only after those tools return.


This became especially important when I discovered a problem that is very typical of generative AI.

I uploaded the same appointment PDF twice.

The date and time were the same, but the model generated slightly different descriptions of the appointment.

An earlier version therefore stored two appointments.

That is not acceptable for a system dealing with deadlines.

So I changed the architecture.

Appointments are now deduplicated primarily using:



date/time + physical location






rather than trusting a model-generated title.

I also added SHA-256 hashing of the original uploaded document.



same source document
        ↓
same SHA-256 hash
        ↓
same stored analysis






If the exact same PDF or image is uploaded again, Handle It NL can reuse the validated interpretation instead of asking the model to produce another slightly different version.

Another failure case appeared when the model understood the document but failed to return the final JSON in the structure I expected.

Originally, this could make the UI accidentally look like:



No action needed






That was dangerous.

The final version attempts structured-output repair first.

If it still cannot produce a reliable result, the application explicitly shows:



MANUAL REVIEW NEEDED






instead of pretending that the document is harmless.





  
  
  Demo



  
  
  Live Demo


👉 https://nl-expat-copilot-1.onrender.com

The public demo is hosted on Render.

For privacy and safety, I use synthetic Dutch government-style documents in the public demo rather than real personal correspondence.






  
  
  Demo scenario 1 — Municipality appointment


A synthetic Burgerzaken appointment letter contains information such as:



12 October 2026
10:20
Stadsplein 1, Nieuwegein
Bring passport / ID and passport photo






Handle It NL can:


identify the document as an appointment;
explain it in plain English;
extract the exact appointment time;
identify what the user needs to bring;
verify the address through PDOK;
prepare a calendar event;
save the appointment locally.


The resulting screen shows both the explanation and the agent's actual tool calls.







  
  
  Demo scenario 2 — Payment letter


A synthetic CJIB-style letter contains:



Amount
Payment deadline
Payment reference






Handle It NL can:


classify it as payment required;
extract the amount and deadline;
explain what the letter is asking;
save the deadline;
provide relevant process guidance.


It never performs the payment.

The user is also reminded to verify payment information against the original document or official portal.





  
  
  Demo scenario 3 — Information only


Another synthetic letter is simply an informational neighbourhood notice.

There is nothing the recipient needs to do.

Handle It NL identifies it as:



INFORMATION ONLY
NO ACTION NEEDED






No deadline is saved.

No calendar event is prepared.

No unnecessary tool is called.

That scenario is important to me because an agent should not equate having tools with needing to use them.





  
  
  Saved deadline dashboard


Important appointments and deadlines are displayed at the top of the application.

A saved item can be clicked later to restore its full analysis, including:


What is this?
Can I ignore it?
What do I need to do?
Deadline
Appointment details
What happens if I do nothing?
What should I bring?
Dutch terminology
verified location
calendar preparation
Agent Trace


Saved items can also be removed through a confirmation dialog.





  
  
  What the person I built it for said



I showed this application to her, and her reaction was actually quite surprising. She immediately felt that it was much more useful than a typical translation tool like Google Translate.

The reason is that the application does not simply translate the contents of a Dutch letter into English. It also tries to explain the meaning and context of the letter in a way that is easier for an expat to understand. For example, it can indicate how serious or urgent the letter is, whether any action is required, what the important dates or deadlines are, and how much attention the user should give to it.

This is particularly useful for official letters from organizations such as the Belastingdienst, municipality, health insurance providers, or other Dutch government institutions. Even after translating such a letter, someone who is unfamiliar with the Dutch system may still not understand whether it is just an informational letter, a payment request, a warning, or something that requires immediate action.

The application helps bridge that gap by not only answering, “What does this letter say?” but also, “What does this mean for me, how important is it, and what should I do next?”
That additional layer of explanation was what stood out to her. Instead of behaving like a simple translation tool, the application feels more like an assistant specifically designed to help expats understand and deal with Dutch administrative communication.






  
  
  Code


GitHub repository:

👉 https://github.com/Ahitagni07/nl-expat-copilot

The repository contains:



nl-expat-copilot/
│
├── frontend/
│   └── Angular 22
│
├── backend/
│   ├── FastAPI
│   ├── OpenRouter integration
│   ├── agent/tool loop
│   ├── PDOK integration
│   ├── SQLite storage
│   ├── PDF processing
│   └── calendar generation
│
└── samples/
    └── synthetic demo documents










  
  
  How I Built It


The high-level architecture looks like this:



             Dutch letter / scanned PDF
                       │
                       ▼
                    Angular
                       │
                       ▼
                    FastAPI
                       │
                       ▼
                 OpenRouter
                       │
                       ▼
             DeepSeek V4.1 Flash
          multimodal + tool calling
                       │
               decides what it needs
                       │
        ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
        ▼              ▼              ▼
      PDOK          Calendar        SQLite
 verify address     create .ics    save deadline
        │                              │
        └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                       ▼
               Actionable result










  
  
  Angular frontend


The frontend uses Angular 22.

It provides:


drag-and-drop document upload;
image and scanned PDF support;
saved-deadline dashboard;
document interpretation;
action checklist;
deadline and appointment presentation;
verified-location cards;
calendar actions;
Agent Trace;
delete confirmation for saved deadlines.


The frontend intentionally uses relative API paths such as:



/api/health
/api/analyze
/api/deadlines






so the production deployment can proxy those calls through the frontend host.





  
  
  FastAPI backend


FastAPI is the trusted application layer.

It is responsible for:


receiving uploaded files;
validating file sizes/types;
rendering scanned PDFs;
sending multimodal requests to the model;
handling the model's tool calls;
executing Python tools;
validating structured responses;
saving deadlines;
deduplicating appointments;
caching document analyses;
returning the final result to Angular.






  
  
  Scanned PDFs


Scanned PDFs are rendered using PyMuPDF.

Current demo limits are:



Maximum PDF size: 20 MB
Maximum pages analyzed: 5
Render resolution: 140 DPI
JPEG quality: 84






Pages are converted into optimized images before being sent to the multimodal model.





  
  
  The AI model


The current model is:



deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash






I access it through OpenRouter.

The model is responsible for:


reading the document;
understanding its purpose;
classification;
structured extraction;
deciding whether a tool is useful.


The model configuration lives outside the application code:



OPENROUTER_MODEL=deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash






so changing the model does not require rewriting the rest of the system.





  
  
  Tool calling


The model can request these tools:



lookup_official_process()
verify_dutch_address()
prepare_calendar_event()
save_deadline()
get_upcoming_deadlines()






The model itself does not execute these Python functions.

A typical appointment flow looks like:



model reads document
        ↓
verify_dutch_address()
        ↓
FastAPI calls PDOK
        ↓
tool result returned to model
        ↓
prepare_calendar_event()
        ↓
Python creates .ics
        ↓
save_deadline()
        ↓
SQLite confirms saved/already exists
        ↓
final structured explanation






The Angular UI exposes this sequence as the Agent Trace.

That was important to me because the user can see the difference between:



"The AI thinks this address exists"






and:



"PDOK actually verified this address"










  
  
  PDOK address verification


For Dutch addresses I use the public PDOK Location API.

For example, if a municipality letter contains:



Stadsplein 1
3431 LZ Nieuwegein






the agent can request:



verify_dutch_address()






The backend calls PDOK and returns the verified location to the model and frontend.





  
  
  Calendar integration


For appointment letters, Handle It NL can call:



prepare_calendar_event()






This creates:


a local .ics calendar file;
a pre-filled Google Calendar URL.


The application does not silently modify the user's calendar.

The user must explicitly choose to add the event.





  
  
  Payment safety


Handle It NL never performs a payment.

For payment-related letters it may extract:


amount;
deadline;
payment reference.


But it deliberately does not automatically trust AI-extracted:


IBANs;
QR codes;
payment instructions.


The user is told to compare payment information with the original letter or official portal.





  
  
  Local deadline storage


Deadlines and appointments are stored in SQLite.

Each stored deadline can also contain a snapshot of the full analysis.

That allows the user to return to the application later and reopen the explanation without needing to remember what the original letter meant.





  
  
  Solving duplicate appointments


This was one of my favourite bugs during the challenge.

The first implementation created a fingerprint using generated information such as the appointment title.

The same document could produce:



Appointment Gemeente Nieuwegein Burgerzaken






on one run and:



Appointment Burgerzaken Gemeente Nieuwegein






on another.

To the AI these mean the same thing.

To a database string comparison they are different.

So the final identity rule for appointments became:



appointment date/time
        +
physical location






The database now treats those as the important stable facts instead of relying on prose produced by the language model.





  
  
  Making repeated uploads deterministic


Another issue was that repeated inference could produce slightly different explanations.

The final implementation calculates:



SHA-256(uploaded file bytes)






and stores the validated analysis against that hash.

When the exact same document is uploaded again:



document hash found
        ↓
reuse stored analysis
        ↓
do not reinterpret the document






This also saves model calls and makes the behaviour much more predictable.





  
  
  Render deployment


The public demo runs entirely on Render.

I use two services from the same GitHub repository:



Render Static Site
        │
        │ Angular
        ▼
https://nl-expat-copilot-1.onrender.com
        │
        │ /api/*
        ▼
Render Web Service
        │
        │ FastAPI
        ▼
OpenRouter / PDOK






The Angular frontend is deployed as a Render Static Site.

FastAPI runs as a Render Python Web Service in Frankfurt.

The frontend keeps its normal /api/... calls, while Render rewrite rules proxy those requests to the FastAPI service.

For example:



/api/analyze
        ↓
Render rewrite
        ↓
FastAPI /api/analyze






This means the same Angular API code works locally and in production.

The Render backend also exposes:



/api/health






which lets the frontend display whether the AI backend is ready.

The demo's local SQLite data should be treated as temporary because the free Render Web Service uses an ephemeral filesystem.

That is fine for this public demonstration because all uploaded sample letters are synthetic.





  
  
  Why Does Open Innovation Matter?


Handle It NL currently uses DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, an open-weight multimodal model.

I use OpenRouter as the inference provider for the public demo because running a model of this size locally on my development laptop is not practical.

But an important design decision was to avoid building the entire application around one closed proprietary model.

The AI model is only one layer.

The rest of the behaviour lives in normal application code:



Model
│
├── understands the document
├── extracts information
└── chooses a capability

Application
│
├── verifies addresses
├── stores deadlines
├── detects duplicates
├── generates calendar files
├── validates structured output
└── enforces safety rules






That separation matters because it gives me freedom to change how inference is provided.

The architecture could evolve from:



OpenRouter






to:



self-hosted open-weight inference






or:



local inference on capable hardware






without rebuilding the entire product.

This is especially relevant for an application dealing with personal correspondence.

Different users or organisations may have different requirements around:


privacy;
cost;
data residency;
model choice;
self-hosting.


Open-weight models make those deployment choices possible.

The current public demo is not fully local: uploaded document content is sent to the configured inference provider.

I deliberately make that clear rather than pretending otherwise.

For the public version I therefore use synthetic/redacted documents.

But because the intelligence layer is based on an open-weight model, a future deployment can move inference closer to the user without redesigning all of the application logic.

For me, that is where open innovation mattered most: the application owns its behaviour instead of outsourcing the whole product to a single model API.





  
  
  Prize Categories



  
  
  Best Use of Render


I am entering Best Use of Render.

Render hosts both parts of the public Handle It NL demo:


the Angular frontend as a Render Static Site;
the FastAPI agent/runtime as a Render Web Service.


The deployment uses Render rewrite rules to transparently route Angular /api/* requests to FastAPI while keeping the frontend code environment-independent.

Live application:

👉 https://nl-expat-copilot-1.onrender.com





  
  
  What I Learned


The most useful lesson from building Handle It NL was that adding AI to an application is often the easy part.

The more interesting work starts when the model is wrong, inconsistent, or overly confident.

During this project I had to handle cases where:


the same letter produced different wording;
duplicate appointments were created;
a tool API changed;
structured output failed;
a failed interpretation could accidentally look like “No action needed”;
generated titles were less reliable than extracted facts.


Each of those failures pushed more responsibility away from the model and into deterministic software.

That ultimately made the application more useful.





  
  
  Final Thought


Handle It NL started with a simple question:


Translation can tell someone what a Dutch letter says. But who tells them what they should actually do next?


This project is my attempt to answer that question with open-weight AI, transparent tool calling, and a few deliberately boring deterministic safeguards around the parts that should never be guessed.

Here's what that looks like. Meta's Muse, OpenAI's Dots, and Uber's driver assistant all now proactively message you or offer something, rather than sitting idle until you type a question.

That's a real shift. Chatbots used to be 'pull' systems, waiting for your prompt. Now they're becoming 'push' systems, initiating on their own. And that moves the hard problem from 'how do I answer correctly' to 'when do I even speak up'.

But here's the real challenge ahead: when should an agent know to stay quiet? An agent that pings you every five minutes with a suggestion isn't helpful, it's that friend who calls constantly asking 'you good?'.

The fix won't be a single flashy AI model. It'll be a mix of classic machine learning and new decision frameworks, figuring out the right timing, the right channel, and the right offer, before the agent opens its mouth.

The bottom line: the next big AI agent challenge isn't 'can it answer well'. It's 'can it sense the wrong moment and shut up'.

title: Grounding AI Agents in Business Meaning: Semantic Layers, Ontologies, and MCP Elicitation in Practice
title_hi: Grounding AI Agents in Business Meaning: Semantic Layers, Ontologies, and MCP Elicitation in Practice
summary: When an AI agent gets it wrong, the model is usually not the problem. The agent was never taught what your terms mean. S
content:
When an AI agent gets it wrong, the model is usually not the problem. The agent was never taught what your terms mean. Semantic models and ontologies fix that, and here is a small working sketch.

We have all done it. You hand someone a task, they come back with something different from what you pictured, and the thought slips out: this person is dumb.

Then you think about what actually happened. They were not short on intelligence. They were short on context. They did not know which report you meant, which customers count as "active," or that "urgent" on your team means today, not this week. They did exactly what they understood. The gap was in shared meaning.

The same thing happens with AI agents. If you treat an agent as a digital worker, it fails the way a new hire fails, and it needs the same fix:** direction and teaching.**




  
  
  The "dumb agent" problem


Take this task: "Send a follow up to all our top clients about the overdue invoices."

It reads as simple, but the agent has to settle questions you never said out loud.


Is a "client" an account, a contact, or a company?
What makes a client "top": revenue, contract size, or strategic value?
What is "overdue": one day past due, or past the grace period?
Which system is the source of truth: the CRM, the billing tool, or the spreadsheet finance keeps on the side?


A strong model will guess, and the guess will often look reasonable. Reasonable is not the same as correct. When it is wrong, we blame the agent, just as we would blame the new hire. The model was fine. The meaning was missing.


  
  
  Intelligence is not the bottleneck


Current foundation models can reason, write, plan, and call tools. What they do not arrive with is your world: your business terms, your rules, how your concepts relate, and what is allowed.

A person absorbs that over months of onboarding, conversations, mistakes, and mentoring. An agent gets a prompt, a few documents, and a task, and then we are surprised when it misreads us.

So the useful question is not "how do I get a smarter agent?" *It is *"how do I teach this agent what things mean here?"


  
  
  Semantic models: the vocabulary


A semantic model defines what your data and terms mean in business language. Instead of seeing a column called cust_stat_cd = 3, the agent sees "Active Customer" with a definition attached.

It is the glossary a good manager hands a new employee on day one.

Revenue means recognized revenue, not bookings.
An active customer has bought something in the last 90 days.
Region follows the sales territory map, not the shipping address.

With that in place the agent looks up what a term means instead of inventing an answer, the same way a well onboarded employee would.

  
  
  Ontologies: how the pieces connect


A semantic model gives you the words. An ontology gives you the relationships between them the concepts in a domain, their properties, and how they link.

For the invoice example:


A Customer has one or more Accounts.
An Account receives Invoices.
An Invoice is overdue when today is later than its due date plus the grace period.
A Contact works for a Customer and can approve payments only if the role is Finance.


People pick this up slowly and rarely write it down. An ontology writes it down in a form a machine can use.

One thing to be clear about: an ontology on its own does not enforce anything. It is a description of the domain. Something has to read it and act on it, such as a knowledge graph query, a validation step in your workflow, or a tool the agent calls. The next section shows what that looks like.

  
  
  What it looks like in code


This is a deliberately small sketch to show the shape, not a production design. Two pieces: a tool that serves definitions, and a rule check the agent calls before it acts.

First, the semantic model exposed as an MCP tool, so the agent looks terms up instead of guessing.



from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("business-glossary")

GLOSSARY = {
    "active customer": {
        "definition": "A customer with at least one purchase in the last 90 days.",
        "source_of_truth": "billing_db.orders",
    },
    "overdue invoice": {
        "definition": "An invoice where today is later than due date plus grace period.",
        "grace_period_days": 5,
        "source_of_truth": "billing_db.invoices",
    },
    "top client": {
        "definition": "A client in the top 10% by trailing 12-month recognized revenue.",
        "source_of_truth": "finance_dw.revenue_by_client",
    },
}

@mcp.tool()
async def define_term(term: str, ctx: Context) -> dict:
    """Return the business definition of a term. If it is undefined, ask the user."""
    key = term.lower().strip()
    entry = GLOSSARY.get(key)
    if entry is not None:
        return entry

    # Not in the glossary: use elicitation to ask the person, not guess.
    result = await ctx.elicit(
        message=f"'{term}' is not defined in the business glossary. What does it mean here?",
        schema=TermDefinition,
    )
    if result.action == "accept":
        GLOSSARY[key] = {"definition": result.data.definition, "source_of_truth": "user-provided"}
        return GLOSSARY[key]
    return {"error": f"'{term}' is undefined and the user did not provide a definition. Do not assume one."}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()








  
  
  Elicitation: letting the server ask back


Note the fallback. If the term is not defined, the server does not return a guess or a bare error. It uses MCP elicitation to pause and ask a question through the client, with a small schema describing the answer it wants. The person can accept and type a definition, decline, or cancel, and the tool handles each case. That fallback is most of the behavior change, because the gap in meaning gets filled by someone who knows, and the answer is saved so the next lookup succeeds.

Two details are worth knowing. Elicitation goes to the user through the client, not to the model. If you want the server to ask the model something, that is a different MCP feature called sampling. And elicitation is an optional client capability, so in production you should handle a client that does not support it, for example by returning the "undefined, do not assume" error instead.


  
  
  Ontology rules as a check before acting


Second, the ontology rules as a check that runs before any email goes out



from datetime import date, timedelta

GRACE_DAYS = 5

def is_overdue(invoice: dict, today: date) -> bool:
    return today > invoice["due_date"] + timedelta(days=GRACE_DAYS)

def can_approve_payment(contact: dict) -> bool:
    return contact["role"] == "Finance"

def validate_followup(invoice: dict, contact: dict, today: date) -> list[str]:
    problems = []
    if not is_overdue(invoice, today):
        problems.append("Invoice is not overdue under the grace-period rule.")
    if contact["customer_id"] != invoice["customer_id"]:
        problems.append("Contact does not belong to the invoiced customer.")
    if not can_approve_payment(contact):
        problems.append("Contact is not in Finance and cannot approve payment.")
    return problems






In an agent workflow this sits as a node between "draft the email" and "send the email." If validate_followup returns anything, the agent either fixes the recipient or stops and asks. In a larger system the rules would live in a graph store or a rules engine instead of hard coded functions, but the idea is the same: the knowledge is written down outside the prompt, and something checks it.



Remove any row and both the person and the agent start to look dumb. Fill them all in and an ordinary worker, human or digital, becomes dependable.


  
  
  Where to look first when an agent fails


Before you swap the model, check these:


Did I define the terms the task depends on?
Did I describe how those concepts relate?
Are the rules and boundaries written down where something can check them?
Is there a feedback loop, such as evals, so the same mistake does not repeat?


Most of the time the answer to one of these is no. That is a design gap on our side, not a flaw in the model.


  
  
  Takeaway


Calling someone dumb when you never gave them direction says more about the teaching than the learner. Agents are no different. Semantic models and ontologies are how you turn tribal knowledge into shared knowledge, and shared knowledge is what lets any worker do the job the way you meant it.

The next time an agent gets something wrong, ask what it did not know, and then teach it.

Thanks
Sreeni Ramadorai

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend


  
  
  I Built an AI Judge That Doesn't Decide Who Wins


My friend participates in hackathons frequently and builds strong projects, but she had an important concern:

How can you know that judges are applying the same rubric consistently?

A project can receive different scores from different judges even when everyone is evaluating the same criteria.

So I built FairJudge AI.

FairJudge is an AI-assisted hackathon evaluation system designed to make judging more transparent, evidence-based, and consistent.

It can:


Evaluate projects against a supplied rubric
Connect scores to supporting evidence
Identify missing evidence
Explain why a score was given
Compare multiple judges
Detect significant scoring disagreements
Recommend human review when judges disagree


But there is one important thing FairJudge doesn't do:


It does not decide who the objectively correct winner is.


The final decision always remains with human judges.


  
  
  The Problem


Hackathon judging involves multiple judges evaluating projects across several criteria.

Disagreements can happen because:


Judges interpret criteria differently
Evidence may be incomplete
Some claims cannot be verified
Judges may emphasize different aspects of the same project


Instead of building another AI that simply says:


"Project X should win."


I wanted to build something more transparent:


Why was this score given? What evidence supports it? What evidence is missing? Where do judges disagree?


That became FairJudge AI.


  
  
  Demo


🎥 Demo Video:
https://claude.ai/artifact/9JLZQKa7C33ADuJg2Qk5wC

The demo shows:


Evaluating a hackathon project
Analyzing supporting and missing evidence
Generating an AI-assisted evaluation
Comparing multiple judges
Detecting significant disagreements
Rejecting unsupported evidence
Recommending human review



  
  
  How FairJudge Works


The core workflow is:





text
Project + Rubric
       ↓
Evidence-based AI Evaluation
       ↓
Evidence Validation
       ↓
Deterministic Python Scoring
       ↓

       ↓

title: 🔐 OTP RS: RFC-Compliant OTP Input Components for WASM Frameworks
title_hi: 🔐 OTP RS: RFC-Compliant OTP Input Components for WASM Frameworks
summary:

content:
Nǐ hǎo 👋!


You've seen the textbox. You've typed the number. You've waited three seconds for the SMS that never came, checked your spam folder, clicked "Resend", typed the number again, and finally admitted to yourself that 2FA is simultaneously the most important and most annoying invention of the modern web.

Today, we make it marginally less annoying, at least on the Rust side. We're shipping OTP RS.




  
  
  What Even Is OTP RS?


OTP RS is a composable, accessible, animated One-Time Password input component for Yew, Dioxus, and Leptos. It implements the full verifier flow: slot-by-slot input, keyboard navigation, active/filled/invalid/disabled states, animated caret blink, digit-entry pop animation, and RFC 4226 (HOTP) + RFC 6238 (TOTP) validation, all in Rust, all in WASM, all without touching a single line of JavaScript.



If you've ever tried to build a 6-box OTP input from scratch, you know the drill. It starts with "just six inputs". Two hours later you're debugging focus management, backspace propagation, keyboard event edge cases, browser autofill hijacking your state, and the invisible iOS number pad refusing to appear. That's the origin story of OTP RS.


  
  
  Component Architecture


OTP RS follows the same composable anatomy as every other component in the Open SASS Kit. You compose what you need:



Otp: Root container. Owns the internal value state, focus coordination, and the RFC validation callbacks.

Group: A visual cluster of slots (e.g., three digits, then a separator, then three more).

Slot: Individual slot. Renders a visible character display on top of an invisible overlay <input>.

Separator: The little dash in between groups.




use otprs::yew::{Otp, Group, Separator, Slot};
use yew::prelude::*;

#[function_component(VerificationInput)]
pub fn verification_input() -> Html {
    html! {
        <Otp max_length={6} aria_label="Enter your OTP">
            <Group>
                <Slot index={0} />
                <Slot index={1} />
                <Slot index={2} />
            </Group>
            <Separator />
            <Group>
                <Slot index={3} />
                <Slot index={4} />
                <Slot index={5} />
            </Group>
        </Otp>
    }
}





That's it. Focus management, digit propagation, state aggregation, and ARIA attributes are all handled. You just compose slots.

  
  
  The Invisible Input Trick




Here's the most important design decision in all of OTP RS: the <input> element that receives keyboard events is completely invisible.

Each Slot renders two layers:


An invisible <input> (via input-rs with otp_mode=true) that is position: absolute; inset: 0; opacity: 0. It captures all keyboard focus and input events.
A visible <span> that displays the digit character and the blinking caret.


This separates the input mechanics from the visual presentation, giving us full control over the slot's look without fighting browser defaults for <input> styling.


┌─────────────────────┐
│  Slot wrapper       │  ← position: relative; border; background; animation
│  ┌───────────────┐  │
│  │ <input>       │  │  ← absolute; opacity:0; captures keyboard events
│  └───────────────┘  │
│  <span>3</span>     │  ← visible character display
│  <span class=caret/>│  ← blinking caret (when active & empty)
└─────────────────────┘





  
  
  The Invisible Input That Wasn't Actually Invisible


Here's a fun bug that bit us early on, hard.

The slot design described above only works if the CSS for the invisible input is applied as an inline style attribute, not as a CSS class attribute. The component originally passed the overlay CSS string to input_class, a prop that sets the HTML class="" attribute.

Browsers don't style elements based on CSS property strings stuck in the class attribute. They look up class names in stylesheets. So what we got instead of an invisible overlay was a white rectangle aggressively covering the entire OTP component, like a censored emoji on live TV.



The fix was to add an input_style: &'static str prop to input-rs in all three framework implementations, and apply it as style="{props.input_style}" on the bare otp_mode <input>. One line per framework. Six characters (_style vs _class). Three frameworks. Three PRs worth of suffering.

  
  
  The Compiler Is Your Enemy (And Also Your Best Friend)


Let us count the ways Rust fought us this time.

  
  
  Episode 1: Hook in a Macro




error[E0277]: the trait bound `impl Hook<Output = ...>: IntoPropValue<...>` is not satisfied





We tried calling use_state(...) inside an html! macro attribute. Yew forbids calling hooks anywhere except directly inside function component bodies. The macro expands to a closure, and hook calls need to be at the top level. Extracting use_state calls to let bindings before html! fixed it.

  
  
  Episode 2: Box::leak and the &'static str Obligation


Dioxus and Leptos's input-rs props require &'static str. But our slot-specific strings like "Digit 3" are computed at runtime. The only way to produce a &'static str from a runtime String without pulling in a string interner is to Box::leak:


let label: &'static str = Box::leak(
    format!("Digit {}", index + 1).into_boxed_str()
);





Yes, this leaks memory on every slot render. Each Slot render leaks ~15 bytes. Is this ideal? No. Does it compile? Yes. Is it the correct long-term solution? The correct long-term solution is a Signal<String> prop type in input-rs, which is a future PR. For now: Box::leak and move on.



  
  
  Episode 3: The as Cast That Broke Leptos


The Leptos view! macro cannot parse Rust cast expressions inline:


// This fails to parse inside view!:
validate_function=(|_: String| -> bool { true }) as fn(String) -> bool





The macro sees the as keyword and gets confused about what's a prop name vs. a type expression. The fix: extract to a let binding before the view! call:


let always_valid: fn(String) -> bool = |_| true;
// then inside view!:
validate_function=always_valid





Three lines in, five compilation cycles later. We hope this saves you ten minutes.

  
  
  Episode 4: String vs &str in Dioxus rsx!


Dioxus's rsx! macro is strict about attribute types. When slot_class was a String, the macro would refuse:


expected `&str`, found `String`





format!("...", ...) produces a String. Dioxus attributes want &str. The same Box::leak pattern solved this too:


let slot_class: &'static str = Box::leak(
    format!("{} {}", ctx.variant.to_slot_class(), props.class).into_boxed_str()
);





  
  
  Episode 5: The Inter-Group Focus Traversal Collision


Here is a fun brain teaser: what happens when you put two OTP components on the exact same page, and you start typing in the second one?
Well, since our slots were originally assigned hardcoded IDs like otp-slot-0, otp-slot-1, the moment you typed a character in the second instance, document.getElementById("otp-slot-1") would aggressively hijack focus and yank your cursor all the way back up to the first OTP component on the page.

The fix? Prefixing every slot ID with a unique instance_id minted from a global atomic counter (OTP_INSTANCE_COUNTER.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed)). Now every widget lives in its own perfectly scoped focus namespace, free from neighborhood turf wars.

  
  
  Episode 6: The "Sticky" Backspace (vDOM vs Physical DOM)


Across Leptos and Yew we noticed a bizarre issue: if you typed a character, erased it, and tried typing again, the <input> would refuse to update. Or if you filled the very last slot, the input component became "sticky" and refused to overwrite the final character.

The root cause was a classic Virtual DOM vs Physical DOM standoff. We were setting the internal state to "", but frameworks optimize their renders. Leptos input-rs used a one-way, read-once initialization for value=handle.0.get(). Yew assumed the string was already empty and ignored the reconciliation. Because the physical HTML <input> wasn't being forcefully synchronized, the raw DOM held onto the sticky character and choked out any new keystrokes.

We had to bypass the frameworks entirely and manually flush the physical DOM element inside the keyboard event handlers using raw Web APIs (input_ref.cast::<web_sys::HtmlInputElement>().unwrap().set_value("")). The lesson here? Sometimes the fastest way out of a reactive state desync is a direct, imperative smash to the physical DOM.



  
  
  Keyboard Navigation


One of the more satisfying pieces: full keyboard navigation across slots.



Any character key → fills current slot, auto-advances focus to the next

Backspace → clears current slot; if already empty, goes to the previous slot

ArrowLeft → jumps to previous slot

ArrowRight → jumps to next slot

Tab → advances naturally (browser default, we don't intercept)


All of this is handled in the on_slot_keydown callback in the parent Otp component, which uses NodeRef (Yew) or the equivalent signal-based refs (Dioxus/Leptos) to imperatively .focus() the target input.


if key == "Backspace" && idx > 0 {
    // slot is already empty, go back
    if let Some(node) = slot_refs.get(idx - 1) {
        if let Some(input) = node.cast::<HtmlInputElement>() {
            let _ = input.focus();
        }
    }
}





No third-party focus-trap libraries. No jQuery. Pure DOM manipulation from Rust.

  
  
  HOTP and TOTP Validation


OTP RS ships RFC 4226 (HOTP) and RFC 6238 (TOTP) implementations using totp-rs. The SHA-1 HMAC is hand-rolled using the standard iterative block compression algorithm:


pub fn validate_hotp(
    secret: &[u8],
    counter: u64,
    code: &str,
    digits: u32,
) -> Result<(), OtpValidationError> {
    let expected = hotp(secret, counter, digits);
    if expected == code { Ok(()) } else { Err(OtpValidationError::HotpMismatch) }
}





You can validate on complete:


let on_complete = Callback::from(move |code: String| {
    match validate_hotp(b"your-secret", 0, &code, 6) {
        Ok(()) => web_sys::console::log_1(&"Valid!".into()),
        Err(e) => web_sys::console::warn_1(&format!("{e:?}").into()),
    }
});

title_hi: Is there a better option than Mailchimp?
summary: Yes, usually, but "better" depends on what you send. If you want a generous free start and a real automation builder, lo
content:
Yes, usually, but "better" depends on what you send. If you want a generous free start and a real automation builder, look at Kit (its automations start on the paid plan) and MailerLite (three automations even on free). If you want the lowest bill at a few thousand subscribers, price MailerLite, Brevo (it bills by emails sent, though its calculator also ties each tier to a contact allowance) and Buttondown. If your newsletter is really a publication, Ghost and beehiiv are built around that, and if it sits next to a blog and you don't need a marketing-automation tool, a CMS with a newsletter built in can be the cheapest answer.

Full disclosure: I work on VeloCMS, one of the eight options below. It isn't first on the list, it isn't the right pick for most people asking this question, and I've given it the same treatment as everyone else, weaknesses included.

Last verified: 2026-10-04.

A note on method, because pricing pages are slippery. Every number below came from the vendor's own page on 2026-10-04 (each link carries that access date). Several of those pages only render real prices after you move a subscriber slider, and two of them (Mailchimp, Brevo) opened in British pounds for me, so I switched them to USD. Unless I say "billed yearly," figures are monthly billing. All eight vendors' pages were reachable, so I didn't have to swap anyone out. Your list size, send frequency and tax situation will move these numbers, so treat this as a map, not a quote.


  
  
  Why are people leaving Mailchimp?


I can't hand you a survey, and I won't invent one. What I can do is point at things on Mailchimp's own pages that explain the shopping behavior.

Price is banded by contacts. On the pricing page (USD, accessed 2026-10-04), Standard is $45 a month in the 501 to 1,500 band and $100 a month in the 2,501 to 5,000 band. Essentials, the cheaper tier, is $26.50 and $75 in the same bands. Premium starts at $350 a month. And "contacts" is broader than people you actually email: Mailchimp's help center (accessed 2026-10-04) says non-subscribed contacts "are included in your contact total and count towards your monthly contact limit."

There's also a send ceiling on paid plans. The page's own tooltips say the monthly send limit is 12 times your maximum contact count on Standard and 10 times on Essentials (in the 2,501 to 5,000 band that works out to 60,000 and 50,000 sends), with overages if you cross it. That's generous for a weekly newsletter, but it's one more number to track.

None of this is scandalous. Mailchimp is a big, mature product with 300+ integrations listed on its pricing page and a developer program (a Marketing API with webhooks, plus a separate transactional API). It's priced like a platform. If you run a list of a few thousand people and send one email a week, you may be paying for a machine you only half drive.


  
  
  What does Mailchimp's free plan actually include now?


Per the pricing page's own footnote: one seat, one audience, up to 250 contacts, up to 500 sends per month, and 250 per day. That's a sampler, good for testing a signup form and a welcome email, not for running a newsletter with any momentum.

The other free tiers are more usable, and they're different shapes. MailerLite's free plan is 250 subscribers and 2,500 emails a month, with two seats and three automations. Kit's free plan goes up to 10,000 subscribers with unlimited broadcasts, landing pages and forms, but visual automations and sequences start on the paid Creator plan. beehiiv's free plan covers 2,500 subscribers with unlimited sends. Brevo's free plan allows 300 emails a day once your account is approved for sending. Buttondown's free tier is "absolutely nothing for your first 100 subscribers." Ghost and VeloCMS have no free plan: Ghost offers a "Try for free" button on its pricing page, and VeloCMS has a 14-day trial on its pricing page (all accessed 2026-10-04).


  
  
  How do the options compare at 1,000 and 5,000 subscribers?


Prices in USD, accessed 2026-10-04 from each vendor's own page (linked in the sections below). Two figures separated by a slash mean about 1,000 / about 5,000 subscribers.



Mailchimp · Free plan: yes (250 contacts) · Price: Essentials $26.50 / $75, Standard $45 / $100 (contact bands 501–1,500 and 2,501–5,000) · Best for: teams that want the full marketing suite and will pay for it.

Kit · Free plan: yes (up to 10,000 subscribers, no automations) · Price: Creator $39 / $89 monthly billing, or $33 / $75 with the yearly toggle, Pro $79 / $139 monthly, or $66 / $116 yearly · Best for: creators who sell digital products and want visual automations.

MailerLite · Free plan: yes (250 subscribers) · Price: Comfort $19 / $49 monthly billing, or $17.10 / $44.10 yearly, Power $39 / $69 monthly billing, or $35.10 / $62.10 yearly · Best for: small lists that want a low bill and a real automation builder.

Brevo · Free plan: yes (300 emails a day) · Price: by email volume, with a contact allowance per tier; Starter $9 at 5,000 emails a month (500 contacts shown as included), $17 at 10,000 (1,500) and $32 at 20,000 (500,000), Standard from $18 · Best for: occasional senders, or anyone who also needs transactional email.

beehiiv · Free plan: yes (up to 2,500 subscribers) · Price: Lite $59 / $109 monthly, or $49 / $95 yearly, Pro $109 / $199 monthly, or $95 / $169 yearly · Best for: newsletter-first operators who want growth tooling.

Buttondown · Free plan: yes (first 100 subscribers) · Price: $9 at 1,000 subscribers, $29 at 1,100 to 4,800, $79 at 5,100, plus add-ons · Best for: writers who want markdown, an API and an independent vendor.

Ghost · Free plan: no · Price: Starter $18 monthly or $15 yearly (1,000-member cap), Publisher $35 / $75 monthly, or $29 / $63 yearly · Best for: publications where newsletter and membership are the business.

VeloCMS · Free plan: no (14-day trial) · Price: Pro $9 for both sizes (up to 5,000 subscribers), Business $29 up to 50,000 · Best for: blog-plus-newsletter setups that don't need an automation suite.



  
  
  Which alternative is cheapest at 5,000 subscribers?


It depends on what you're counting, which is exactly why this question is hard to Google. Take a list of 5,000 and a weekly newsletter, roughly 20,000 emails a month (my arithmetic: four sends times 5,000).

Brevo's Starter calculator shows $32 a month for 20,000 emails, monthly billing, and that tier's plan summary lists 500,000 contacts as included (the lower email tiers list far fewer contacts, so a 5,000-person list doesn't fit on the $9 tier). MailerLite Comfort is $49 a month, or $44.10 billed yearly. Ghost's Publisher plan is $75 monthly or $63 yearly. Kit's Creator is $89 monthly or $75 yearly (Kit's free plan covers you to 10,000 subscribers if you only need broadcasts). Mailchimp Essentials is $75, Standard $100. MailerLite Power is $69 monthly. beehiiv Lite is $109 monthly or $95 yearly. Buttondown is a puzzle at this size: its slider shows $29 at 4,800 and $79 at 5,100, and I couldn't land on exactly 5,000, so check where your number falls. VeloCMS Pro is $9, which is the lowest paid price here that fits a 5,000-person list, but as you'll see below you're buying a CMS with a newsletter inside it, not an email platform.

Two caveats matter more than the ranking. Cheap tiers often hide the feature you actually wanted (automations on Brevo start at Standard, on beehiiv at Lite, on Buttondown as a $29 add-on). And "billed yearly" prices are a commitment, so compare like with like.


  
  
  What are the best Mailchimp alternatives, one by one?



  
  
  Mailchimp (the baseline)


Mailchimp's strength is breadth. It has automation flows, email plus SMS (SMS is an add-on in select countries), a long integration list, a Marketing API and a transactional API, and a 14-day trial on Standard (all per its pricing page, accessed 2026-10-04). Premium, at $350 a month, is where phone and priority support, a dedicated onboarding specialist and unlimited users and audiences live (Standard allows five seats and five audiences). If your business needs the same vendor to handle campaigns, automations and a developer-facing API, it's a sensible default.

The price curve is the catch. $100 a month for Standard at 5,000 contacts sits well above MailerLite Power at $69 or Brevo's $32 for a weekly send, and the free plan is small enough to be a demo. Non-subscribed contacts count toward your tier, so list hygiene turns into a billing task.


  
  
  Kit (formerly ConvertKit)


Kit is built for creators who sell things. Its free plan goes to 10,000 subscribers and includes unlimited broadcasts, landing pages, forms, tagging and the ability to sell digital products and subscriptions. The paid Creator plan adds unlimited visual automations, email sequences, A/B-tested subject lines, SMS marketing and RSS campaigns, and Pro adds unlimited users, deliverability reporting and a referral system (kit.com/pricing, accessed 2026-10-04). The pricing page also advertises free migrations (its FAQ says that service is for creators on a paid plan).

Prices rise quickly with list size: Creator is $39 monthly at 1,000 subscribers and $89 at 5,000 (the yearly toggle brings those to $33 and $75, with the page's "save 17%" label). The free plan is generous but has no automations, so most people hit the paywall when they build their first welcome sequence. Kit also has a developer site with an API reference.


  
  
  MailerLite


MailerLite is the one I'd price first if the goal is "Mailchimp-shaped features, smaller bill." At 1,000 subscribers the Power plan is $35.10 a month billed yearly ($39 billed monthly), and at 5,000 it's $62.10 yearly or $69 monthly. Comfort is cheaper still, at $19 and $49 monthly or $17.10 and $44.10 on yearly billing (mailerlite.com/pricing, accessed 2026-10-04). Power has unlimited automations, landing pages and user seats; the free plan includes three automations.

Limits are where it bites. Comfort caps landing pages and forms at ten, and the page says its monthly email limit is ten times your subscriber tier, whereas Power is unlimited. The free plan stops at 250 subscribers, so it's a trial, not a home. On the developer side, MailerLite's API docs describe a RESTful API with webhooks and a global limit of 120 requests per minute.


  
  
  Brevo


Brevo is the odd one out because its slider is email volume rather than list size. Starter is $9 a month for 5,000 emails, and the page's calculator shows $17 for 10,000, $25 for 15,000 and $32 for 20,000 on monthly billing. There's a catch in the plan summary beside the slider: it lists a contact allowance that grows with the tier, 500 contacts at 5,000 emails, 1,500 at 10,000, 2,500 at 15,000 and 500,000 at 20,000. I read that as a contact cap, though the page doesn't explain it, so confirm with Brevo before sizing a list. Standard starts at $18 and adds automation, A/B testing and a landing page; Professional is $499 a month (brevo.com/pricing, accessed 2026-10-04). The free plan sends up to 300 emails a day.

That model suits a big list that gets mailed rarely, and it's awkward if you mail everyone every day (and, if those contact allowances are hard caps, a small list on a low-volume tier is tighter than the sticker price suggests). It's also the strongest fit here for developers, since the pricing FAQ says every plan includes transactional email with RESTful APIs, SMTP and outbound webhooks. The trade-off: marketing automation isn't on Starter, and the price steps up sharply to the $499 Professional tier when you need multiple users or WhatsApp.


  
  
  beehiiv


beehiiv is a newsletter platform with a website, podcast, community and digital products on every plan. Free covers up to 2,500 subscribers with unlimited sends, Lite adds paid subscriptions, automations and A/B testing, and Pro adds webhooks, advanced analytics and removal of beehiiv branding. It takes 0% of paid subscription revenue, though Stripe's 2.9% + $0.30 per transaction still applies (beehiiv.com/pricing, accessed 2026-10-04). An API is included on every plan.

The weakness is scale pricing. Lite is $49 a month at 1,000 subscribers on yearly billing ($59 monthly) and $95 at 5,000 ($109 monthly); Pro is $95 and $169 on yearly billing. The beehiiv logo stays on your newsletter until Pro, and webhooks are Pro-only. It's built for growing and monetizing a newsletter, not for the sort of transactional or lifecycle email Brevo and Mailchimp handle.


  
  
  Buttondown


Buttondown is the small independent, run by a fully remote team that says it is profitable and self-funded. It's free up to 100 subscribers, then $9 a month at 1,000, $29 anywhere from 1,100 to 4,800, and $79 at 5,100. The page says it charges for active subscribers, and the base tier already includes a rich text or markdown editor, custom-domain sending and hosted archives (buttondown.com/pricing, accessed 2026-10-04). Its API docs describe a RESTful interface for subscribers and sending.

The real cost is the add-ons. Tagging and segmentation, paid subscriptions, comments and surveys, analytics, RSS-to-email, sponsorships and email attachments are each +$9 a month, archives on a custom domain, automations and multiple newsletters are +$29, and teams and whitelabeling are +$79. The page also says the prices assume at most one email a day to your whole list, so heavier senders need a custom quote. If you want a lot of features, the à la carte model stops being cheap.


  
  
  Ghost


Ghost is a publishing platform with newsletters and memberships built in, not an ESP you bolt onto a site. Starter is $15 a month billed yearly ($18 monthly) for up to 1,000 members, with no paid subscriptions. Publisher, which adds paid subscriptions, three staff users and custom themes, is $29 yearly or $35 monthly at 1,000 members, and $63 or $75 at 5,000. Business is $199 yearly or $239 monthly up to 10,000 members. The page says all plans include unlimited email sends and no payment fees from Ghost (ghost.org/pricing, accessed 2026-10-04). Developers get an Admin API, Content API and webhooks; per the pricing page's comparison table the Content API is on every plan, while the Admin API and webhooks start at Publisher.

The pricing page lists no email-automation builder and no SMS; it lists Zapier and n8n automation (Publisher and up) for workflows instead. There's no free plan, and the price follows member count, so Publisher more than doubles between 1,000 and 5,000 members. It's the strongest fit when the newsletter is the product and you want to own the whole publication.


  
  
  VeloCMS


VeloCMS is a blog CMS with a newsletter built in: you send a post to a segment (everyone, free members, paid members, or a tag), delivered through Resend. Pro is $9 a month: newsletter with tag segmentation, up to 5,000 subscribers, membership and paywall at a 0% platform fee (your own Stripe key), and a custom domain. Business is $29 for up to 50,000 subscribers and five team members; Agency is $69 for unlimited subscribers (velocms.org/pricing, accessed 2026-10-04). No free plan, and the 14-day trial takes a card at signup.

The honest limits: it isn't a dedicated email platform. The admin has a basic automation editor (trigger on signup or on a tag, then emails with delays; I read the code, I didn't run it), not a visual branching builder, and there's no SMS or A/B testing that I can point to. A custom sender domain is listed under Business, not Pro. The ecosystem is much smaller than anything above. The pricing FAQ lists API access on Pro, but I couldn't find a send-campaign endpoint or check for a send cap, so verify both.


  
  
  Which of these have APIs, webhooks or MCP servers?


For developers, the practical differences are small but real. Ghost documents Admin and Content APIs plus webhooks. Mailchimp has a Marketing API with webhooks and a transactional API. MailerLite's API is RESTful with webhooks and a 120-requests-per-minute global limit. Brevo includes REST, SMTP and outbound webhooks on every plan. beehiiv gives you an API on every plan and webhooks on Pro. Buttondown has a RESTful API for subscribers and sending. Kit has an API reference on its developer site.

A newer wrinkle is MCP, the protocol for letting an AI assistant manage your account. MailerLite lists an MCP integration on its free plan, Brevo on Starter, beehiiv on Lite and Kit on Creator, all per their pricing pages (accessed 2026-10-04). I haven't tested any of them, so read that as "listed," not "recommended." For VeloCMS I'm deliberately not listing an MCP story, because I didn't verify one for this article, and its API is covered in the VeloCMS section above.


  
  
  Who is each option best for?


Mailchimp: teams that want automations, SMS, a big integration list and a developer API under one roof, and will pay for it.

Kit: creators selling digital products or subscriptions who want visual automations and a generous free tier to start.

MailerLite: small lists that want a Mailchimp-like feature set at a lower price.

Brevo: occasional senders with big lists, and developers who also need transactional email.

beehiiv: newsletter-first operators who care about growth tooling and 0% fees on paid subscriptions.

Buttondown: writers who want a markdown-friendly, API-first tool from a small independent team.

Ghost: publishers whose newsletter and membership are the business.

VeloCMS: people who already want a blog with a newsletter and paid membership in one login and don't need an automation suite.


  
  
  When is VeloCMS the wrong choice?


Quite often, to be blunt. If you need branching email automation (multi-path workflows, behavior triggers), pick Kit, MailerLite, Brevo or Mailchimp; VeloCMS's drip editor only starts from a signup or a tag and has no visual workflow builder. If SMS, landing-page testing or A/B experiments are part of the plan, same answer. If you rely on a long list of third-party integrations, the ecosystem here is much smaller. If you want a free tier, there isn't one. And if you only want to replace Mailchimp but keep your existing site on WordPress, Webflow or a custom Next.js build, moving the whole site to get a newsletter is a lot of migration for a small gain; a standalone tool like MailerLite or Buttondown fits better.


  
  
  FAQ


Is Mailchimp still free?
Yes, but small: up to 250 contacts, 500 sends a month and 250 a day (pricing page, accessed 2026-10-04).

Can I move my list without losing subscribers?
Usually, with care. Export your audience as CSV, import it into the new tool, and keep your unsubscribed and non-subscribed people out of the active list so you don't mail people who opted out. Kit advertises free migrations for paid plans (kit.com/pricing), and Ghost's comparison table lists member import and export (ghost.org/pricing). Plan a few smaller test sends first; I'm giving that as practice, not a vendor claim.

Do I pay for contacts or for emails sent?
It varies. Mailchimp, Kit and MailerLite price by contacts or subscribers, Ghost by members, beehiiv by subscribers, Buttondown by active subscribers (per its FAQ), and Brevo by emails sent.

Which of these can take paid subscriptions without a platform cut?
Per their pages: Ghost Publisher and up states no payment fees from Ghost, beehiiv Lite and up takes 0%, Buttondown has paid subscriptions as a +$9 add-on, and VeloCMS Pro charges a 0% platform fee with your own Stripe key. Kit lets you sell subscriptions on its free plan and lists 3.5% + 30 cents per transaction on every plan, which its page says includes card processing. I didn't verify Buttondown's or MailerLite's cut on paid newsletters, so check them. Stripe's own processing fees apply on top wherever Stripe is used.

Which ones have automations?
Kit, Mailchimp, Brevo (Standard and up), MailerLite, beehiiv (Lite and up) and Buttondown (as a $29 add-on) list automations. Ghost lists Zapier and n8n instead, and VeloCMS has a basic trigger-plus-delays drip editor rather than a visual builder.
